title: Additional partners join nuclear-powered LNG ship project
html:
Under the agreement - signed on 20 November at DNV's headquarters in Høvik, Norway - the project partners will develop a nuclear-powered LNG carrier vessel concept, designed for operation on a route between LNG terminals in the USA and Europe. The first steps of the project involve the partners working together to set out a roadmap that will outline the concept for the demonstration vessel and a plan for safety assessment and approval, all with a view to realising a practical commercial pathway for the design, construction, and commissioning of the ship.

Samsung Heavy Industries of South Korea will lead vessel concept development and marine integration, including shipbuilding feasibility and construction methods. US nuclear technology company Tesser Atomics will lead the reactor technology and nuclear plant development, as well as the reactor-specific safety and licensing work. Norwegian classification society DNV will contribute its expertise in maritime safety, risk assessment and classification, including hazard identification, a safety assessment framework and a classification and verification roadmap. Meanwhile, the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) will coordinate the research, funding proposals, build the project consortium, support feasibility studies, as well as working on simulations, modelling and testing.

The vessel concept is built around the integration of Tesser's Triton, a compact fluoride-salt-cooled high-temperature reactor (FHR) designed for ships. The company says the reactor pairs proven tri-structural isotropic (TRISO) fuel with low-pressure molten salt coolant and online refuelling, in a nuclear module small enough to fit the ship and powerful enough to propel it.

The Demonstration Project 1 (DP1) will serve as a reference for SFI SAINT - Norway's nuclear-powered vessel research centre. The project will be one of multiple demonstration projects conducted in coordination with the Norwegian University of Science and Technology-led SFI SAINT centre.

"This additional agreement is important because it fills out the team that will develop DP1, and defines roles and responsibilities," Per Peterson, co-founder and CEO of Tesser Atomics, told World Nuclear News. "NTNU acts as the project manager, enabling the DP1 demonstration project to benefit from and coordinate with the SFI SAINT consortium", of which Tesser is a member.

The latest agreement came a day after Tesser entered into an exclusive strategic collaboration with Samsung Heavy Industries on the DP1 project. Under that MoU, Samsung Heavy Industries becomes Tesser's exclusive shipbuilder partner, while Tesser becomes Samsung Heavy Industries' exclusive reactor partner for the demonstration project.

"Our ability to work with the Norwegian SFI SAINT consortium has accelerated our progress across all of the areas one must address to deploy our first nuclear-powered demonstration ship, including legal, regulatory, and insurance," Peterson said. "Our partnership with Samsung Heavy Industries brings world-class expertise and capabilities in ship design and construction for our demonstration project."

Kyunghee Kim, Executive Vice President and Head of the Future Business Division at Samsung Heavy Industries, added: "Nuclear-powered vessels are one of the promising eco-friendly alternatives for transportation amid the global trend toward decarbonisation. Building on the technology and experience we have accumulated in the field of marine small modular reactors (SMRs), we will establish a meaningful stepping stone toward the commercialisation of nuclear-powered vessels together with partners that have expertise in their respective fields."

Ivar Håberg, Director of Approval Ship Classification at DNV, said: "One of the interesting things about nuclear power for shipping is that we have a long track record of use in the naval segment, but that this has not translated into the commercial sector. That makes this project an important step towards the first modern full-scale nuclear-powered cargo vessel. DNV is very proud to be working with partners that are focused on what it takes to realise this project, especially on the shipbuilding side. It is also another example of how the Norwegian maritime cluster, by combining support for innovation with a strong focus on safety, is well positioned to help move the maritime industry forward."

"Norway has a long history of innovation in maritime technologies, from the early development of LNG carriers to our work today in SFI SAINT to develop and demonstrate commercial nuclear propulsion," said Hans Petter Hildre, Chair of the Norwegian University of Science and Technology Department of Ocean Operations and Civil Engineering. "Norway already licenses visits by thirty to forty nuclear-powered naval vessels to Norwegian ports each year based on safety reviews by our nuclear safety authority, DSA. We look forward to supporting this nuclear-powered LNG carrier demonstration project."
